title: Games that use LLM in an original way?
author: JedahVoulThur
selftext:
Nothing wrong with that, just curious if you are developing a game, or know any that uses an LLM as something else than a chatbot to talk with characters or to generate the story in real time, which are the most common uses I've seen around.
I know that the reason they are used for that is because precisely that's what they are good at, but that's not the only thing LLMs are good at. For example, has anyone created a game that uses LLMs for processing data, maths or procedurally writing code while the game is running? Imagine using an LLM together with a behavior tree as the "brain" for an enemy in a strategic game. Is even something like that possible?

comments.author: SurvivalHermit
comments.body:
Something i want to try and i think would be really good would be to build the game on specetimedb then give the LLM a ton of telemetry data and let it translate the telemetry data into an internal narrative and then change DB values to change things about the game world based on that narrative.  
  
AI is a really good obfuscation layer for triggers because it is imprecise  and will not always make the same decissions twice given the exact same input data. Given proper sanity checking and per change limits a fairly low parameter LLM could have a great impact on making a world feel like it is slowly reacting to the player and what is happening in the world.

comments.author: GaiusVictor
comments.body:
There is a bunch of games that use LLMs, alongside normal code, to provide a TTRPG-like experience, but with content that's customized and/of created on the fly.

I've tried a bunch of them, but the two whose names come to mind at the moment are AIRPG and Myth.OS.

AIRPG is by far the most developed of the category but still feels kinda meh to me. Myth.OS is still in relatively early development but already feels more powerful than AIRPG. I'm still trying it out but the reason why I like it is because it offers you to tools to customize your campaign with a granularity I haven't yet seen others do.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
I've been exploring non-generative uses of AI, in my case, as a kind of game engine component. Even very small/simplistic AI can provide a surprisingly decent substrate for mechanics design.   
  
In terms of the "ship of theseus" kind of game you describe it's really interesting - something only vibe coders would've expeienced so far, I imagine, but you can see it becoming more common in future.   
  
I once had a card game that was quite simple, and had fairly modular mechanics, as well as placeholder assets for when adding new cards, etc. At one point, I asked an LLM to introduce three new cards, but not tell me wha the mechanics were, etc. At that point I was playing against it, quite like you describe. But it's not really, a good way to design games. It was more of a fun experiment trying to figure out what had changed etc.

comments.author: chcampb
comments.body:
Honestly offline LLM is going to be the way to go for quite some time. 

If you think about most transcendentally large games, like BG3 or FFXIV or something, seriously go read the discussions from interviews on how they did ARR, it's all about the process. The process to handle immense quantities of data to make the game. LLMs are good at doing that, to the point where they can easily organize and manage it. But importantly this frees humans up to create memorable interactions, which the AI can then fill in the gaps.

For example, let's say your gameplay involves several situations (again think BG3) where each of those situations changes the world state. Things your NPCs say need to consider that world state, or even where they need to be (refugees, etc). The more complex you make that, the richer the world is, but the longer it takes to develop. Hence taking a very long time to develop BG3, or similar games, which 

But imagine turning an LLM over to take your notes and fill in all of the nuanced, contextual discussions which are all things you wrote - but you don't have time to go out and cross reference every combinatorically growing combination of situations. 

LLMs used offline will create the capability to make larger and more consistent, rich games than have been made before.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: I stay far away from giving players access to my LLM, out of fear of that "your game got popular overnight, here's a $30k bill".

replies.author: Morph_Games
replies.body: Yeah, LLMs need to come down in price dramatically before they can be used for games. Crypto games had the same problem: an ongoing service cost. It means your game needs to be a subscription -- which is very hard to pull off, especially for experimental indie games.
